# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.

- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.

- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

screens.why5: It keeps my act, following what hearing people said, and my rungs, and nothing about the glasses leaks into it.
screens.why7: All five rungs grade one measure, how much of the talk was followed; the order runs from the working rung 'Followed everything that was said' to the outright failure 'Could not follow it at all'; the line after 2 puts 1 to 2 against and 3 to 5 for, so the belief can be both supported and refuted; and the bar names a rung that is on the final list.

screens.why1: Picking who asks the questions comes naturally right before the study goes out, after the problem rows are checked.
screens.why2: Two names with a play button and a plain note on cost and delivery; I can read it at once.
screens.why3: I can play two 5-second clips and pick, so it sits fully within what I can do.
screens.why4: For deaf and hard-of-hearing people, the choice I'd most want is missing: a text-only interviewer, or a face shown clearly enough to lipread with captions on, not just one voice or another.
screens.why5: It keeps my 'deaf or hard-of-hearing adults' and leaks nothing of the glasses to the people answering.
screens.instead: Who should ask deaf or hard-of-hearing adults your questions? Daphne (on video, captioned, face clear for lipreading) / Saskia (same) / Text only, no video, with a note that every question is always written on screen.

screens.why1: Choosing how my deaf and hard-of-hearing respondents answer belongs right after picking who asks, just before sending, and it matters a lot for my people.
screens.why2: Each option says plainly what the respondent will see and do, and I can choose on first reading.
screens.why3: I know my users well, so I know that for many of them a spoken video interviewer is a barrier and reading on a screen is not.
screens.why4: The three choices are complete and distinct, but the voice-first Daphne option only works for my audience because the questions are also written, and 'speak into it' is a slightly odd offer to many Deaf respondents, though typing covers it.
screens.why5: The screen keeps my actor wording and leaks nothing about the glasses or captions to respondents.
screens.instead: How should deaf or hard-of-hearing adults answer? Read and tap (type in boxes) / Daphne on video with every question captioned on screen / Let them choose

screens.why1: After choosing who interviews and how they answer, deciding who receives the link is the obvious last step before sending.
screens.why2: The three choices read plainly on first pass; 'Contacts page' is Keel's own term but explained in place.
screens.why3: I know whether I have named deaf and hard-of-hearing users I can reach directly versus a community group I'd post in.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover my real options, though the first option's sub-line is first person ('I send') while the second switches to 'you send', a small wobble in voice.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product, roles or wording is altered or leaked; it is purely about distribution.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? -- People I know by name (I send each one their own link) / A list I found with Keel (Keel makes a link for each; I send them) / A group, with one open link (I post it where they already are, e.g. an HLAA chapter or Deaf community group).

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'People disagree' sits beside 'median 4 days out of 7', but a median of 4 is inside my 4-to-7 claim, so the number shown seems to support me; the number that actually decides it (4 of 7 against a bar of 5, one short) is only down in the card.
screens.why_b2: Prevalence and Current solution read at once (n of 7 against a bar), but the Frequency card repeats the split three ways and Importance prints '7 of 7 put it in their two' twice, so I have to read those again to find the count and the bar.
screens.why_b3: The four dimension names and belief lines are the ones I checked, in my words: missing what hearing people said, 4 to 7 days out of 7, catching what they say among the two, and today's way falling short.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what a one-short split on frequency means for AirCaps, for example whether to lead with the daily-wearer wedge or to narrow the claim to 2 to 3 days, and 'What it measures' only explains the method.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is visible, but three beliefs are called 'Holding up' on seven answers with no word that seven is a small sample, which reads firmer than the data can carry.
screens.instead: Frequency is one person short of your bar: 4 of 7 hit 4+ days, 3 had it 2 to 3 days. With only 7 people, check whether your daily wearers are a narrower segment, or say 'most weeks' rather than 'most days'.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside its deciding count, 7 of 7 said yes against a bar of 6 of 7, so I know it held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows seven 'for' cells on a 0 to 7 axis, with my marker at 6 labelled 'at least 8 in 10', so what is counted, over how many, and where my bar sits are all plain at first look.
screens.why_b3: 'At least 8 in 10' is my band and the event is recognisably my problem, but the belief line shortens my segment to 'deaf or hard-of-hearing adults' and drops 'in the US who talk with hearing people every week', which is the wedge I chose.
screens.why_b4: 'Common among these 7' plus a pointer to the next two cards is mostly navigation; it doesn't say what a full yes means for my day-one wedge.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is visible throughout, the count line says 'a small group: a lean, not a call', and the So line keeps the claim to 'these 7', so nothing outruns the data.
screens.instead: At least 8 in 10 deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week missed what was said in the last 7 days: all 7 said yes (bar 6), a lean, not a call. The problem is there for your wedge; whether it comes often enough to wear glasses daily is the Frequency card, where people disagree.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'People disagree' sits right beside the deciding numbers: 4 of 7 at or beyond my 4-day low, with a bar of 5 of 7, so it is 1 short.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts days out of 7 over 7 people, and the strip shows 4 for and 3 against with the marker at 5, so all three are plain at a glance, though the 0 tick is a button nobody could press.
screens.why_b3: The dimension is mine and the range 4 to 7 days out of 7 is mine, but 'miss what hearing people said in a conversation' rewords my 'too fast or too noisy to follow'; I recognise it, but it is not quite my line.
screens.why_b4: 'Whether it matters is the next card' sends me on without telling me what a 4-of-7 split means for my wedge, such as whether to aim at the daily-struggle users or lower my band to 2 to 3 days.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is visible and 'a lean, not a call' is honest, but the stray '— the most recent time it happened' after the question suggests a single-occasion question when people were asked for a count of days.
screens.instead: Drop 'the most recent time it happened' from the Asked line, and make the So line say: 4 of 7 hit it on 4+ days, while the other 3 are on 1 to 3 days; your daily-use wedge is real for about half, so either lead with the heavy users or test 2 to 7 days.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside its deciding number, 7 of 7 put it in their two against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The bars and the bar marker read at once, but the caption says '7 people · each picked two' while the bars add to 13 picks, not 14, so I have to stop and work out that one person picked only my row and then 'Nothing else'.
screens.why_b3: The card's title is Importance and the belief carries my circumstance, my people and my own difficulty, 'Catching what hearing people say', which is what my glasses are for, along with the rivals I named.
screens.why_b4: The So line usefully warns that being in the top two is not ranking first, but it never says what that means for AirCaps, such as leading the pitch with catching speech or noting that getting a word in (3 of 7) is the runner-up worth watching.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible and the card calls 7 people 'a lean, not a call', but 'each picked two' is a small claim the 13 picks contradict.
screens.instead: 7 people · 13 picks (one picked only yours) -- all 7 put catching what hearing people say in their two; a lean from 7, so keep it as the lead problem and watch 'getting a word in', picked by 3, as the next pain.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside its deciding number, 6 of 7 said today's way falls short against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: Each rung shows its count, my line under 'Missed only a little' is drawn and labelled, and the strip shows 6 for, 1 against and the marker at 5 over 7 people, so all three read at first look.
screens.why_b3: The title and the shape of the belief are mine, but the act reads 'following what hearing people said'. My job was to follow and join a face-to-face conversation, so the 'join' half and the face-to-face setting are gone, though I still recognise it.
screens.why_b4: The So line names the gap (3 caught only the gist, 3 missed most of it) but then only says my solution is judged against it on the next study, which could sit on any card and doesn't tell me what that gap means for the glasses.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is visible everywhere, the count line calls it 'a small group: a lean, not a call', and the So line keeps to 'these 7', so nothing claims beyond the people who answered.
screens.instead: Holding up, as a lean: 6 of these 7 lost part of their last conversation (3 kept only the gist, 3 missed most of it), so the next study should ask whether the caption glasses get those six to 'Missed only a little' or better. Tomás, deaf on one side, already manages with seating and may not need them.

screens.why_b1: The box says Holding up with '6 of 7 said today's way falls short · bar 5 of 7' right beside it, so I have both the verdict and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b3: 'Current solution' is my dimension, but 'following what hearing people said still falls short' is a stiff rewording of my job, 'follow and join a face-to-face conversation'; I recognise it, but it isn't how I'd say it.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the screen says what one coper with one-sided loss means for the idea, and the line that actually split, Frequency, gets no why and no next step.
screens.why_b5: The n stays visible and the counts are honest, but the heading 'When a line fails' sits over a line that held, which made me read the result twice.
screens.why_b6: Tomás's end-seat trick is a real workaround, but I already typed seat choice as an importance row; the only new hint is that single-sided loss may sit outside my wedge, and the screen doesn't draw that out.
screens.instead: Current solution held, 6 of 7 (bar 5). The one who copes is deaf on one side only and manages by taking the end seat, so lead with bilateral and severe loss. Frequency is where people split, and it has no why here: ask what makes a week hard.

screens.why1: As the first screen it is obvious why it asks whether I talk with hearing people each week, since the study is about that.
screens.why2: Plain words I would use myself; I talk about hearing people all the time.
screens.why3: I know whether I talk with hearing people every week; I do, at work, at the shops, with family.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it for a gate, and no escape is needed on a screener.
screens.why5: It matches the segment of people who talk with hearing people every week and gives away nothing about any product.
screens.why6: Short and one question, but 'I'll read 2 options. Yes; or No.' is clumsy where the spoken screener should just end 'Yes or no.', and for me the spoken form only helps if it is also captioned.
screens.instead: Do you talk face to face with hearing people every week? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I talk with hearing people every week, it makes sense to ask whether I missed what they said this past week.
screens.why2: Miss what hearing people said is exactly how I'd put it myself, and I'd answer on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know straight away whether I missed what people said at work, at the shop or at dinner this week.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it, and the chips belong to the story box after a Yes, so they aren't a fault here.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product, captions or an app reaches me; it is just about my conversations.
screens.why6: One short sentence then 'Yes or no', easy to take in at once, provided I can see the captions of the AI's voice.
screens.why7: It names the window and one act, but for someone like me missing some of what hearing people say happens nearly every day, so almost everyone in the segment would say Yes and No is left to very few, close to the routine rather than the moment it costs us.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you lose track of a conversation with hearing people and drop out of it? Yes · No

screens.why1: Right after I said yes, I missed something this week, it makes sense to ask how many days that happened.
screens.why2: Missing what hearing people said is exactly how I'd put it, and I get it on first read.
screens.why3: I know which days this week I lost track at work, at the shop or at dinner, so I can count them, though I'd wonder whether missing one word counts.
screens.why4: One button for each day from 1 to 7 plus I can't recall covers every answer I could give, and none of them overlap.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product or company comes through; it's just about my week.
screens.why6: It's short and one question, and 'say a number from 1 to 7' is easy to hold when heard or read in captions.
screens.why7: Every option is a count of days in the 7-day window from 1 to 7 in order, the escape is there and is the only one, and a founder's low of 2 or more would split the buttons for and against.

screens.why1: Right after asking how often I missed what people said, it makes sense to ask which part of that conversation I'd most want made easier.
screens.why2: "Their hearing loss" and "where they can see every face" made me stop: it's my hearing loss and I need to see their faces, so I had to read those two twice to work out who "they" was.
screens.why3: Every one of these is something I deal with myself at a dinner or a meeting with hearing people, so I can answer from last week.
screens.why4: The set covers my real struggles and None of these fits, but two options are written about somebody else ("their hearing loss", "they can see") instead of in my own words.
screens.why5: The third-person wording reads like a company describing "people with hearing loss" rather than talking to me, so their way of naming us leaks through.
screens.why6: Heard aloud it's one question and five short options I can hold, though the "they" in the seat option is a little muddy by ear.
screens.why7: Catching what hearing people say is on the list, not first, with at least two other rows and None of these at the first ask, but choosing a seat where I can see faces is mostly a way of catching what's said, a means of the main row rather than a separate difficulty.
screens.instead: Think of your last conversation with hearing people. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Catching what hearing people say · Getting a word in at the right moment · Telling people about my hearing loss · Taking a break from listening without leaving · None of these

screens.why1: After asking how often I missed things and what I'd want easier, asking how my last conversation actually went is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Hearing people, followed, the gist and missed are exactly how I talk about conversations, though 'How did following what hearing people said go?' is slightly clumsy.
screens.why3: I know exactly how my last conversation went, whether I got all of it or nodded along with the gist.
screens.why4: The five run cleanly from everything to nothing, my true answer is always one of them, and 'I can't recall' fits because nobody can follow a conversation for me.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product, captions or the company reaches me; it is just my conversation, in words deaf people use.
screens.why6: One short question with five short parallel options I can hold after hearing them once, then the escape.
screens.why7: All five rungs measure how much of the conversation I followed, from followed everything (today's way working) down to could not follow it at all (failing outright), parallel and in order, so the belief can go either way, with the 'I can't recall' escape the card requires for an act that can't be handed off.
